documents.text:
Regina M. Anderson

Regina M. Anderson (1900-1993) was an American playwright and librarian of multi-racial descent. Born in Chicago, Illinois, Anderson was a prominent figure in the Harlem Renaissance movement of the 1920s and 1930s. Early Life and Career

Anderson was born to a family of mixed racial heritage, with African American, Native American, and European ancestry. She grew up in a culturally rich environment, which would later influence her writing. Anderson pursued a career in librarianship, working at the 135th Street Branch of the New York Public Library, a hub for African American literary and cultural activity during the Harlem Renaissance. Literary Career

Anderson's playwriting career spanned several decades, during which she wrote several plays that explored themes of race, identity, and social justice. Her work was heavily influenced by her experiences as a woman of color and her involvement in the Harlem Renaissance. Anderson's plays were performed at various venues, including the Harlem Experimental Theatre and the Krigwa Players. Personal Life

Regina M. Anderson was married to William T. Andrews, an American politician from New York. Andrews served as a member of the New York State Assembly from 1933 to 1941 and was a prominent figure in New York politics during the mid-20th century. Evidence of Marriage

According to various sources, including the New York Amsterdam News and the Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, Regina M. Anderson was married to William T. Andrews. A 1935 article in the New York Amsterdam News mentions Anderson's marriage to Andrews, stating that "Mrs. William T. Andrews, playwright and librarian, is one of the most talented women of the race." (1) The Schomburg Center for Research in Black Culture, a leading repository of African American cultural and historical materials, also confirms Anderson's marriage to Andrews in its biographical entry on the playwright. William T. Andrews (1898-1984) was an American politician from New York. He served as a member of the New York State Assembly from 1933 to 1941 and was a prominent figure in New York politics during the mid-20th century.
